analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals, nursing homes, and social service employers to run workplace violence prevention plans.
analysis.headline: The bill has 32 Senate cosponsors but has sat in the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee with no hearing, vote, or floor action since its April 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill tells the Labor Department to write a binding workplace violence prevention standard for health care and social service employers, who would have to write prevention plans with front-line workers, assess risks, fix hazards like poor lighting or no panic alarms, investigate violent incidents, log and report them, train staff annually, and protect workers who report violence from retaliation. It covers hospitals, nursing homes, psychiatric facilities, group homes, emergency responders, and workers providing care in patients' homes, and ties Medicare participation for hospitals and nursing homes not covered by federal safety law to following the standard.
analysis.who_benefits: Health care and social service workers: nurses, aides, orderlies, social workers, home health and hospice aides, and emergency responders who face punches, threats, and assaults from patients, visitors, and others on the job. They would gain enforceable prevention plans, security measures like alarms and access controls, annual training, incident investigations, and protection from retaliation for reporting. Patients and the public also benefit indirectly, since safer, better-staffed facilities deliver better care and lose fewer experienced workers to injury and burnout.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health care and social service workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires every covered employer to write and maintain a workplace violence prevention plan developed with direct participation of front-line workers and their representatives, tailored to each facility's actual hazards.

Mandates that employers identify and fix specific hazards — security and alarm systems, access controls, weapon detectors, adequate staffing, and flagging clients with a history of violence — and investigate every violent incident with employee input.
Requires annual training for workers, including before a new hire's first assignment, plus extra training for supervisors and for staff working with trauma or trafficking victims.

Creates a paper trail: violent incident logs kept for at least 5 years and open to employees, annual summaries posted at the workplace, and yearly reports from employers to the Labor Department and from the Department to Congress.
Bars employers from retaliating against workers who report violent incidents, threats, or hazards to the employer, law enforcement, or government agencies.

Extends coverage to home health, hospice, and home-based social work, to emergency responders and firefighters, and — through a Medicare participation condition — to hospitals and nursing homes not otherwise covered by the Occupational Safety and Health Act, such as many state and local government facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, nursing homes, psychiatric and substance-use treatment facilities, group homes, home health agencies, and social service employers bear the cost: writing plans, assessing risks, installing security hardware like alarms and cameras, running annual in-person training, keeping records, and in some cases adding staffing or safety personnel. Costs would be largest for under-resourced providers such as rural hospitals and nursing homes, and some would likely be passed to insurers, government payers, and patients through rates. The Labor Department also pays for writing the standard, building reporting systems, and enforcement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, and care agencies

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on financially strained providers. Nursing homes and rural hospitals operate on thin margins, and requirements for security systems, training, recordkeeping, and possibly more staff could squeeze them or be passed on to patients and payers.

The bill short-circuits the normal federal rulemaking process: the Labor Department must issue an interim final standard without the usual OSHA procedures, with only a 30-day comment period, and exempt from the Paperwork Reduction Act and White House regulatory review.

A written plan does not by itself stop violence. In field settings like home health visits in private residences — where much of the risk occurs — employers can install fewer physical controls, and critics could reasonably worry the plan becomes paperwork rather than protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker-protection payoff is concrete — enforceable plans, security controls, training, and retaliation protection for a workforce with high exposure to assault — while the main cost is compliance spending that many providers already bear in part under state laws like California's, and that can partly pay for itself through fewer injuries and less staff turnover. The genuine trade-offs are the strain on thin-margin nursing homes and rural hospitals, the bypassed rulemaking process, and the limits of paper plans in home and field settings. On balance the bill's benefits to workers are larger than its costs, though a more gradual phase-in for small providers would have addressed the sharpest objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote ever since.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill on April 1, 2025, joined by 21 original Democratic cosponsors including Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren, and Patty Murray.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, chaired by a Republican.
Cosponsorship grew to 32 — 31 of the 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of the 2 independents — but no Republican has signed on.
The committee has taken no further action: no hearing, no markup, and no vote appear in the bill's action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one has gained from a final outcome because the bill is still pending; in the interim, health care employers including hospitals, nursing homes, and home care agencies benefit from facing no new federal violence-prevention requirements, while the workers the bill would protect remain uncovered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Care employers avoiding new safety rules

for.name: Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 21 original cosponsors.

for.name: National Nurses United and nursing unions
for.what_they_did: Have publicly pushed for a federal workplace violence prevention standard for health care workers across multiple Congresses.

against.name: Bill Cassidy
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since its referral.

against.name: Hospital, nursing home, and home care industry groups
against.what_they_did: Have opposed mandatory federal workplace violence standards for health care employers in past Congresses, citing cost and duplicative state rules.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors are Democrats or independents, no Republican has signed on, and no vote has yet occurred to show the full partisan split.

industries.note: They would bear the cost of prevention plans, security hardware, training, logging, and reporting, and Medicare participation would be conditioned on compliance for facilities outside federal safety law. The industry's cost-avoidance interest runs against the workers and patients whose safety the rules would protect.

Residential facilities are explicitly covered and sit at the center of the violence risk the bill targets, so compliance costs would hit an industry already operating on thin margins. Opposition here is a direct trade-off against aide and nurse safety.

industries.industry: Home health and social service agencies
industries.note: Field work in private homes and community settings would require plans, training, and coordination procedures, though physical controls are limited in clients' homes. Their interest in avoiding these costs runs against the aides who face violence alone in the field.

The bill guarantees union and worker representatives a formal role in writing plans, investigating incidents, and evaluating compliance, giving organized labor a standing enforcement foothold that matches its members' safety interest.

industries.industry: Workplace security equipment and training vendors
industries.note: Mandates for alarms, access controls, weapon detectors, and annual in-person training create a large new customer base. The industry profits only by selling what the law requires workers to have.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is unlikely to advance on its own: the Republican-chaired HELP Committee has shown no movement, no Republican has cosponsored, and no Senate vote has ever been taken on a companion version despite the House passing one in two earlier Congresses. Its realistic paths are dying quietly at the end of the 119th Congress or having its provisions folded into a broader health or labor package if the political balance changes.
